To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
cross-immunity and mortality are necessary conditions to sustain oscillatory behavior of age-structured epidemic models.
sustained oscillations are possible in models with age-specific mortalities and cross-immunity, and are not possible in models with constant mortalities.
sustained oscillations of influenza strains can be observed when age-specific mortalities are present, but not if mortality is independent of age.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the interplay between age structure, cross-immunity and infectious disease dynamics.
the interplay of age-specific infection activity levels and cross-immunity, and how this affects the dynamics of co-circulation.
the role of cross-immunity and the age-structure of the host population on the observed dynamics of the co-circulation between influenza subtypes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

sustained oscillations are not possible for the two-strain model without age-specific mortalities and cross-immunity; and are possible for the two strain model in the presence of cross-immunity and either age-specific mortalities or activity levels.
sustained oscillations in the co-circulation between influenza subtypes are possible in the presence of cross-immunity and a realistic age structure.
cross-immunity is not the sole cause of observed oscillations.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the age structure, cross-immunity and proportionate mixing in the models can lead to sustained oscillations in the disease dynamics.
the age structure and cross-immunity are important for understanding the co-circulation and oscillation of influenza subtypes.
age-specific mortalities and cross-immunity can lead to the observed co-ciruculation of influenza strains.
The main takeaway from our work is that
cross-immunity and mortality rates are important factors in understanding the co-circulation dynamics of H1N1, H3N2, and other influenza subtypes.
the interplay of cross-immunity, mortality rates, and age structure may be a key factor in determining whether or not sustained oscillations are observed.
the interplay of cross-immunity and mortality rates can produce oscillatory dynamics.
